desc:
There are k identical machines and durations[i] is the running time of job i. Every job runs on exactly one machine without interruption; a machine runs one job at a time, starting at time 0 and never idling between its jobs. You decide which machine takes each job and in what order.

The completion time of a job is the time at which it finishes. Return the minimum possible sum of the completion times of all jobs (0 if there are no jobs).

durations = [3, 1, 2], k = 2  ->  7

Run 1 then 3 on one machine (finishing at 1 and 4) and 2 on the other (finishing at 2): 1 + 4 + 2 = 7.
hints: For a single machine the jobs should simply run from shortest to longest. Why?

On one machine the last job's duration is counted once, the second to last twice, and so on: a job with m jobs behind it (including itself) is counted m times. With k machines you have k slots of each multiplicity.

Sort the durations in decreasing order. The k longest jobs get multiplier 1 (they run last on their machines), the next k get multiplier 2, and so on: the job at sorted index i contributes duration * (i // k + 1).
editorial: The duration of a job is added to the completion time of itself and of every job after it on the same machine. So a job that has m - 1 jobs after it on its machine is counted m times in the total. Every machine offers one position with multiplier 1 (its last job), one with multiplier 2, and so on, so the multiset of available multipliers is k copies of 1, k copies of 2, ... Each multiplier is used from 1 upwards, because filling a larger multiplier while a smaller one is free is never better.

To minimize the sum of duration × multiplier, pair the largest durations with the smallest multipliers (rearrangement inequality). After sorting durations in decreasing order, index i gets multiplier i // k + 1. Time O(n log n); the largest total is below 2.1·108 (k = 1, n = 2000).
